data.text/markdown:
Model profiles for the spike short

The trade. A liquid stock gaps up 0.25–1.0 ATR, runs +5% from the open, and we short on the first red 1-minute bar, covering 20 minutes later. We make money when the spike fades. We lose big when it keeps running (a continuation loser, here any trade at or below −200 bps). The job for a model is almost always the same question: is this one of the 1-2 shorts a day that will keep running? Different models answer it from different inputs:
Model Reads Answers Speed Status here
LightGBM numbers about the trade (51 features) P(tail loser) µs tested
CatBoost same, handles categories natively P(tail loser) µs tested
TabPFN v2 same, no training loop (in-context) P(tail loser) ms–s tested
Chronos-Bolt the price path so far future price paths ~10 ms GPU tested
Kronos OHLCV candles sampled candle paths ~0.3 s CPU tested
CLM-8B text (news, filings) + a list of options nearest option ~100 ms not run yet
Jev any structured state + typed questions a pick, a score, a yes/no ~0.5–1 s API demo'd (Jev notebook)
Every chart below uses saved results from this lab unless it says illustration.

Build a filter by hand

Each line is one short. Drag along any axis to keep only part of its range (for example slow run-ups, or entries near the high); drag axis titles to reorder. The scorecard under the chart recomputes for whatever survives, so you can see straight away whether a filter helps on the holdout periods as well as on the tune year.
575 of 575 shorts pass the brushed filter

LightGBM: the workhorse

What it is. Gradient-boosted decision trees. Fast to train, fast to score, strong on tables of numbers. Good at. Mixing many weak signals (run speed, distance from the high, red-bar volume, SPY/QQQ) into one risk score, and finding interactions a human rule misses. Where it fits. At the arm: score each short before entry and veto (or size down) the riskiest ones. Microsecond scoring means it can sit inside a Rust runner. What we found. Out-of-sample AUC 0.63–0.71 for tail losers, the steadiest of the three tabular models. Vetoing the riskiest 20% still left profit factor at 0.72–0.91. It ranks; it doesn't rescue. Chart. The raw ingredients it combines. Fast runs (low minutes_to_trigger) and entries far below the high are the strongest tells.

CatBoost: categories and stability checks

What it is. Another boosted-tree model, built to handle categorical inputs (sector, catalyst type, weekday) without one-hot encoding, with ordered boosting that resists target leakage. Good at. Mixed tables where labels matter: catalyst = strong positive earnings next to price features. That makes it the natural home for Chris's news taxonomy once it's frozen. Where it fits. Same gate as LightGBM, but trained with the red/yellow/green catalyst label as a feature. What we found. A warning about overfitting: profit factor 1.01 on the tune folds fell to 0.58 on Q3 2026, then 0.83 in Oct-Nov. Without the catalyst column it has little to add over LightGBM.

TabPFN v2: a model that doesn't train

What it is. A transformer pre-trained on millions of synthetic tables. You hand it your labelled trades as context and it predicts the new ones in one forward pass, no tuning loop. Good at. Small samples. We have ~1,200 training trades and ~180 tail losers, which is exactly the regime where boosted trees overfit and TabPFN tends to shine. Where it fits. A quick second opinion for any new edge Mark proposes: a baseline in minutes before anyone tunes anything. Also useful for rare categories like strong positive earnings shock (5 cases so far). What we found. Best tune AUC (0.67) but it slid to 0.65 forward and profit factor 0.64. Runs in a separate worker process because torch and LightGBM clash on macOS.

Chronos-Bolt: a price-path forecaster

What it is. Amazon's time-series foundation model (T5-style), trained on many kinds of series. Give it the 1-minute closes so far and it returns forecast quantiles for the next 20 minutes. Good at. Reading the shape of a run without any feature engineering, and giving a range, not a point. Where it fits. As one more input to the gate: "how high could this still go?" (the q90 path max). If the upper band is far above the arm price, the spike may not be done. What we found. Weak. AUC 0.68 on tune, 0.54 forward. The pre-entry window is only 2-45 bars (our data starts at 09:30), which is thin context. Worth retrying with 30-second bars and pre-market. Chart. Red dots should sit to the right if the forecast worked. They're mixed in.

Kronos: a candlestick language model

What it is. A model that tokenises OHLCV candles the way an LLM tokenises words, trained on billions of candles from many exchanges, then samples plausible next candles. Good at. Sampling many futures. The share of paths that keep running is a direct, explainable risk number: "12 of 16 simulated futures went another 2% higher". Where it fits. Pre-entry risk score, or a size multiplier, and a nice visual for the replay notebook (draw the 16 paths on the chart). What we found. No reliable edge: AUC 0.51-0.56 on the holdouts for P(path reaches +200 bps). CPU speed ~0.3 s per trade with 16 paths. Same thin-context problem as Chronos. Chart. On all 575 lab trades Kronos flags about 15% of continuation losers and 5% of the others: a real but small tell that misses most of the damage.

CLM-8B: pick the nearest answer

What it is. A contrastive language model (Qwen3-8B base) that embeds a question and a list of options in the same space and picks the closest. No text generation, so it's fast and its choice is easy to audit. Good at. Sorting text into a fixed menu: which of Chris's 11 catalyst categories is this headline?, which past event looks most like this 8-K? Where it fits. Pre-open, on every headline and filing for the 400-name universe. Jev: fast, typed decisions

What it is. A decision model (TypeSafe's System One) that never writes prose. You give it a state and typed questions (yes/no, pick one, score 0-1) and it answers in under a second, cheaply, with a confidence. Good at. Judgement calls that rules can't express but that must be fast and auditable: is this headline about the ticker?, grade this catalyst, should this order pause? Where it fits. Everywhere a human would glance: the pre-open red/yellow/green screen, a confidence gate at the arm, a news kill switch during the 20 minutes, and tagging the cause of each loss afterwards. Putting it together: ranking skill is not profit

Every model and combination on the two holdout periods. Moving right (better ranking) barely moves anything up. Tail losers and winners look too alike at the moment of entry, so the next gains probably come from new inputs (the protected-limit entry, 30-second bars, catalyst labels from CLM-8B / Jev) rather than new models.
